=== NEW - Bicep language for deploying resources ===


--- The anatomy behind building an Azure virtual machine ---

Now, in this chapter, I just want to give a kind of a simple introduction over the concept of the
virtual machine service.
Again, this is just for the benefits of those students who are not familiar with these base services
on Azure.
The Virtual Machine service allows you to host virtual machines without the need of buying and maintaining
the underlying physical hardware.
And here, the best thing about this service is you only pay based on the usage of the service itself.
In the past, if a company had to host a set of applications, they would first need to invest money
in buying servers, buying storage, setting up different aspects in the background like networking,
cooling, etc. they would need to build data centers.
All this was an upfront cost for the company itself.
They would then host their Applications.
Then we had the advent of virtualization.
In virtualization on your physical server, you would install virtualization software, a hypervisor.
With the help of this hypervisor, you could start building virtual machines.
So you could have multiple machines now running on a single physical server.
The virtual machines would use the hardware of the underlying physical server itself.
Now the advantage was that you could have multiple applications running on these virtual machines,
and you could make use of the capacity of the underlying physical server itself.
But here again, the problem is that in order to start using virtualization, the company still has
to buy the underlying physical hardware in terms of what in terms of either the physical servers, the
storage, the software, etc. there's a lot of work that needs to be done just to get the virtual machines
in place for hosting your applications in Azure.
With the help of the virtual machine service, the underlying physical infrastructure, the hardware
is maintained by Azure themselves from Microsoft.
All you have to do is you have to deploy your VMs and start using them.
The company does not need the overall burden of, you know, investing in buying physical hardware,
in buying storage, etc. they go onto the cloud, onto Azure.
They say, I want to build a virtual machine.
I want to deploy a virtual machine onto my account, and within a matter of minutes, you'll have the
virtual machine up and running.

--- Understanding Azure regions ---

Hi and welcome back.
Now in this chapter I want to briefly go through Azure regions.
When you decide to deploy a resource based on a service, one of the important decisions that you need
to make is what is the region to host your resource.
There are certain services that are available at the global level where you don't need to choose a region.
But for most services, you need to decide a region.
So what is an Azure region?
So this is a set of one or more data centers in a specific geographic location.
Here the data centers are connected by high capacity, low latency networks.
When you deploy resources onto Azure, you deploy them onto a region.
Remember for us, when we deploy a VM, I told you in the end it would need to be on some sort of physical
server in a data center.
Just giving an example screenshot here.
So when you deploy the VM.
The machine is deployed to an underlying physical host in Azure Data Center.
If you look at the manage disk, the OS level disk, these are stored on Azure storage clusters.
If we look at your virtual network, this is again part of some sort of physical networking system.
There are decisions that impact the region of choice.
So for example first is the latency and user experience.
So is it for me.
East US is not the ideal location in terms of latency and user experience because it's further away
from me.
If you have users who are going to use an application hosted on a VM, then choose a region that's closest
to your users.
See, when you make a request to an application on a VM, right, the request still needs to go to the
data center in that region which is hosting the VM itself.
And the response needs to come back.
Hence there is a latency.
It takes time.
So normally companies would decide to host the virtual machine in a region that's closest to them.
That's one aspect of choosing a region.
Another aspect is compliance.
Maybe due to legal and security implications, you might need to host your data within a particular
region.
If you have a VM that's hosting an application, and an application is storing application data on the
VM itself, you might need to ensure that the data is due to, again, certain security implications.
It has to be in a particular region.
Another one is features and pricing.
Now if you look at the virtual machine service.
So this is the basic service in Azure.
It is available in all regions.
And in terms of all of its features also it's available in all regions.
But it's not the case that each and every service is available in each and every region.
So if you're using a service you first have to go on to the Microsoft documentation to make sure that
that service is available, or its features are available in a particular region.
So even if you do decide that you want to host your resource based on a service in a particular region,
you still have to make sure that the service is available in the region itself.
So this is important.
Another thing is the pricing.
So the pricing of a service depends on region to region.
The price per r in our case let's say for an Azure VM in East US, let's say I'm my VM is in East US.
The price per R for the VM in East US will be different from the price per R of the VM in North Europe.
A company might decide to choose a region wherein the cost is minimal.
So even the pricing also is a factor in terms of deciding on a region.
If you want to just have a quick look at the global infrastructure.
Into the global experience can actually go on to data centers.
Docs.microsoft.com.
Here you will see all of the different regions across the world.

--- Azure Virtual Machine - Disks ---

Hi and welcome back.
Now in this chapter, I want to kind of give an introduction and a focus on Azure.
Manage this when it comes onto our VMs.
By default they get an OS level disk.
Here you have the operating system files.
If you install, let's say an application or a workload on the VM itself.
If you want to store application data, then it's better to actually go ahead and create an additional
disk.
The Azure managed disks are block level storage volumes that are managed by Azure themselves.
These are like your physical disks that you have for your machines, but they are virtualized when it
comes onto the virtual machine environment so that you get that OS level disk.
But what you can do is you can create additional data disks and then you can attach them onto your VMs.
I say this is ideal when you want to host applications.
So if your applications need to store their data instead of storing them on the OS level disk, it's
normally recommended to store it on a separate data disk.
Now, when it comes on to manage data disks, there are different types of disks in place.
We have currently, at this point in time different types.
So we have standard HDD, standard SSD, we have the premium SSD and we have Ultra Disk.
SSD is basically backed by solid state drives.
These are data disks are much faster in nature.
They give you higher performance depending upon the type of workload that you're going to host on your
VM, you will decide on the type of disk.
So for example, if you want to host a lightweight web server on a VM and that web server needs to store
its web data, the web application.
You can create an additional data disk based on, let's say, standard SSD.
You will see for each disk the maximum disk size, something known as max IOPs and max throughput.
Obviously, the cost of having a disk in place is going to increase based on the feature, right?
If you look at ultra disks, these really give you the best performance.
And this is ideal when you have production level database systems in place, when you need better performance,
better throughput.
At that point in time, you'll probably use Ultra Disk, but again, the cost is going to increase.
And the cost obviously based on the amount of provisioned throughput, we are going to go on to a lab
on how we can add a data disk onto VMs.
But before that, You can go through this documentation link to understand your decision in terms of
choosing a particular disk type.
And before that, I want to give kind of a quick note when it comes on to IOPs and throughput.
So each disk type you get a certain number of IOPs in place and throughput.
What exactly is IOPs?
So IOPs is the physical input and output operations per second for storage.
Let's say that you're hosting a database server on a VM.
On the database server you host a database and tables of information.
The CPU of the VM is obviously required from a computational aspect for the database server, but the
data itself, the data in the tables.
Finally, in the end they are stored as database data files on the underlying hard disk.
Okay.
On the disk itself.
Now, when a user fires a query against the database system, let's say to fetch data from an underlying
table, what's going to happen is first the database server.
That service is going to see if that table data is already in memory.
In order to serve the data, in order to serve the data from the database.
The data first needs to be loaded onto the internal Ram memory.
So if the data is not present in the Ram memory, it's present on the data disk.
Then the database service needs to perform a read operation and input operation on the data disk copied
onto memory, and then give the response of the query back to the user.
Hence, this concept of an input operation of reading data from a disk.
Okay, it's an operation.
This is the amount of IOPs in terms of input.
If you are writing data onto the disk, its output operations for a database system, a production database
system, you will have a million queries in place that's going against the database service itself.
At that point in time, the database server might be doing a lot of operations on the underlying disk.
So at that point in time, the amount of IOPs that is supported by the disk is very, very important
because if the IOPs is less then the it would become a bottleneck for the database service to go and
fetch data.
So this is very important.
It all depends also on the amount of IOPs based on your requirement.
The other thing is throughput.
Now throughput is the amount of data per second that the disk can accept or give.
An example is let's say you have an application hosted on the VM.
That application accepts videos uploaded by users.
Now, videos are basically big chunks of data.
If you look at a database system, there are queries are small chunks of data.
But here we are looking at, let's say videos in different resolutions.
They are big chunks.
They are big video files.
These videos, when they are uploaded by users, they have to be copied onto the underlying data disk.
If you have a higher throughput, you can copy larger chunks of your video.
Hence, you'll get a better throughput in terms of copying videos onto the underlying data disk.
Again, this is very beneficial if you have applications that are taking in a lot larger chunks of data
as input and then copying it onto the underlying data disk, it's going to give kind of a quick overview
on IOPs and throughput because these are key factors.
But for us we're going to go simple.
We are just going to see how to basically create an additional data disk and attach it onto VM in the
subsequent chapter.

--- Azure Disks - Server Side Encryption ---

On this topic, I want to give an introduction onto something known as encryption when it comes onto
your disk.
See when you look at our infrastructure.
So when it comes on to virtual machines, rbms are hosted.
Remember on physical servers in Azure Data Center.
When it comes onto our disks.
So for us these disks are virtual in nature.
But in the end these disks are hosted on some sort of storage cluster, right?
This is physical hardware.
These are storage scale units or clusters or racks of storage nodes.
So in the end you have to remember that your disk is your virtual disk.
The data is stored on actual physical hardware.
And remember everything is part of a data center in the end.
From an Azure perspective, Microsoft, they have a lot of security protocols in place to secure your
data.
So in terms of physical access, in terms of security for your softwares, etc., everything, there's
a lot of security in place.
But companies always want to have that additional level of security.
And here we are talking about data that's stored on the underlying disk.
So you could have sensitive data stored on the disk even though the disks are stored in the end in storage
clusters in Azure data centers, where it's not easy to get access to.
From a security perspective, they would want to securely store this data.
That's why you have this concept of encryption.
Encryption is a technique that's used to encrypt data.
You encrypt data using something known as a key and encryption key, and an encryption algorithm when
it comes onto Azure Disk Storage.
They already have something known as server side encryption, enabled by default.
This encrypts the data stored on Azure Managed Disk, both your OS level disk and your data disk.
Your manager, your Azure manages the entire encryption process.
The data is encrypted using an algorithm and a key.
This does not impact the performance of your managed disks and there is no additional cost.
The.
By default, Azure manages the encryption keys.
These are known as platform keys, but you can also make use of your own customer managed keys.

--- Custom Script Extensions ---

Hi and welcome back.

What is the main purpose of Custom Script Extensions is it's a feature that allows you to automate the
post deployment of, let's say, software applications on your machines.
See, what we have done earlier on is when we looked at building VMs.
So we spun up a VM, let's say based on Windows Server or Ubuntu.
And then we logged on to each machine.
Right.
Either it was RDP into the Windows Server or Secure Shell onto the Linux machine.

This was a manual task.
In today's world there's a lot of automation in place wherein we want to automate tasks wherever possible.
So we want to automate the task of installing internet information services on windows.
So when a new VM is deployed automatically, that VM should have internet information services.
Or if we deploy a VM based on ubuntu automatically it should have nginx in place.
And what we can do is one option in Azure is to make use of custom script extensions.

These extensions extend like the name does imply.
It can extend the functionality of certain aspects about your VM.
So first thing is custom script.
Custom script allows you to run scripts that can probably set up an application, set up a software,
install something.

--- Availability Sets ---

Hi and welcome back.
So in this chapter I want to go through the concept of availability sets.
In the last chapter I talked about that overview of, you know, the need of adding stability to your
entire systems and an infrastructure layer when it comes on to your virtual machines.
We do have some features in place for adding, you know, higher availability to your infrastructure.
In this chapter, I want to go through the use of something known as availability sets.
So again, let's take the use case example where in a company is hosting an application on just a single
Azure virtual machine.
I told you, if you have a very critical application running on the machine, and if the machine goes
down, the application is no longer available.
It can result in a loss of revenue and a loss of customer confidence, so on and so forth.
Hence, you want to ensure that the application is always running.
Hence you want to make sure that it's tolerant to faults at different layers.
Told you that the application can go down on its own due to several reasons the application could cause
problems on the VM.
The VM could go down.
The VM can also go down for other reasons at the infrastructure layer.
See for example, we know that the virtual machine in the end is hosted on a physical server in an Azure
data center.
There could be faults in the underlying physical layer, so they could be probably a network issue,
a power issue.
If this is the case, then it would cause a problem to the physical server and hence cause a problem
to the virtual machine.
I said Azure makes sure that their infrastructure is always, you know, highly available, but no one
can guarantee a complete 100% availability for infrastructure, Although sometimes Microsoft has to
perform vital updates to their physical machines, these physical machines again are hosting your virtual
machines.
Sometimes when these updates are applied, it would require a reboot of the entire physical server.
Now, if a reboot is required of the physical server, even though it is a fraction of a time, it could
just take a few minutes.
But in that few minutes, your application will no longer be available because your virtual machine
will be down again.
It's a problem for a company if they are having a critical application in place, a critical application
running on the VM.
So what companies normally do is they increase the availability of these critical applications by making
sure that they have multiple machines in place.
So they'll have the application running on multiple Azure VMs.
So if one machine were to go down, the application would still be available on another machine.
But the problem is that when you launch a VM, you have no control over what physical server the VM
is located on.
Let's say that both machines are launched on the same physical server in the Azure Data Center.
Again, we have that same problem wherein if there is a power failure that impacts this particular physical
server, both machines are down.
Or when Microsoft needs to perform an update on the physical server itself.
Again, both machines are down.
So what you can do is you can distribute your machines across your physical infrastructure by placing
them as part of something known as an availability set.
So what exactly is an availability set?
An And a baby set is a logical grouping of machines that helps you reduce the chances of multiple VMs
going down because of hardware issues.
To make use of availability sets, you need to deploy a machine to the availability set itself.
The machine can only be part of the set when it is created, so you can't add.
Currently, an existing machine has part of an availability set.
So when you create the machine at that point in time, you have to make the machine part of an availability
set.
So how does availability sets actually help in the case of these power failures?
In terms of whenever Microsoft needs to perform an update on the underlying physical infrastructure.
So when a machine is made part of an available set, the machine is allocated on something known as
a fault and an update domain.
So a baby.
Sets are made up of various fault and update domains.
What is a fault domain?
A fault domain defines a group of machines that share a common power source and network switch.
What are update domains?
Update domains are used to signify the group of machines and physical hosts that can be rebooted at
the same time.
So let's say that a company, you know, they have an application that is being used extensively.
Hence they have six machines in place just for the application itself to make sure that you have high
availability.
I said, if you want to deploy these six machines has they were maybe they might be located on the same
physical server and have the same problem at the infrastructure layer.
But if you make these machines part of an availability set, the availability set has different fault
and update domains.
means.
So when the machines are made part of the available set, they are allocated to different fault and
update domains.
So let's say out of these six machines, two machines are part of fault domain zero.
So at the infrastructure layer let's say there's a problem with the power supply and Ethernet switch
off just for domain zero.
It would only impact these two machines.
It will not impact the other machines.
So at fault layer you are trying to isolate the issues when it comes onto the power supply.
You know, things such as the power supply networks such as etc. by placing the machines as part of
different fault domains and at the same time the machines are placed as part of different update domains.
So when Microsoft needs to publish updates to the physical servers, the updates are made to, you know,
each update domain at a time.
A b domain zero could be one set of physical servers.
So when the updates need to go as part of this update domain, it only impacts this particular virtual
machine.
When the updates are done to this update domain, then the updates go on to the next update domain.
So this machine will be up and running and the updates will then impact this machine.
But in the end you still have machines available because they are part of other update domains.
When you create an available set, you can decide on the number of fault domains that you want and the
number of update domains.
Now note that there is no additional cost for using a vary sets.
Obviously from a costing perspective, right?
You are only again charged based on the number of machines that you have running as part of your entire
system.
Now, in the next chapter, I want to showcase how simple it is to go ahead and create machines as part
of an availability set.

--- Azure virtual machine scale sets ---

Hi and welcome back.
Now, in the next series of chapters, we're going to go through a powerful service known as Azure Virtual
Machine Scale Sets.
But before that, I want to give you all a scenario.
Try and explain what's the purpose of this particular service.
Why do we need scale sets?
Let's say a company is running an e-commerce application on a VM.
It's a web application.
Users from the internet are using the application.
Now, over time, users might start to increase the amount of traffic coming in starts to increase,
and because of the load on the application, your machine might start running into memory issues or
CPU issues and your application starts getting performance bottlenecks, etc. what you can do is you
can perform the act of vertical scaling.
In vertical scaling, you can, as we know, resize the VM.
So for example, if you have a size at this point in time of two virtual CPUs and eight gigs of Ram,
you can choose another size that gives you a higher amount of virtual CPU and a higher amount of Ram.
You can implement this very easily.
The only problem is, at some point in time, the machine might need to restart in order to take this
higher configuration.
There is but a problem.
You know, if your load again continues to increase and increase, and you keep on trying to scale up
in terms of vertical scaling, you reach a point of diminishing returns wherein the size no longer has
kind of an impact on improving the performance.
You start paying more just for the size of the machine.
And I said every time you try to resize, there'll probably be a restart required on the machine itself.
In such a case, what you can do is you can look at the concept of horizontal scaling.
In horizontal scaling, you now add multiple VMs as part of your infrastructure.
On these VMs, you have your same web application running and now users, you know the traffic from
the users on the internet.
They can be distribute using something known as a load balancing service that we'll look at later on.
The traffic can be routed across these multiple VMs.
So now your traffic, your load can be different across multiple virtual machines.
It is your responsibility to make sure that you spin up these multiple VMs.
It is your responsibility to ensure that these VMs have your application in place.
But you can achieve better performance by the sort of horizontal scaling where you have multiple VMs.
But now the question arises, how do you manage the adding of these machines onto your architecture?
And why is this a concern?
Because in terms of user traffic, it's not always the same.
Maybe during the daytime it's at its peak, but during the nighttime the traffic decreases.
Let's say for example, at peak you have four machines running your web application as part of your
infrastructure.
Okay.
And at the night time, obviously the load has decreased.
And it only starts the next day.
What you have to understand, you know, from a company's perspective, is when you have more and more
machines running as part of your infrastructure, your cost is also increasing.
Remember, you're spending for the compute now of these machines.
You are spending for the underlying dis spending for other aspects.
When it comes onto the infrastructure itself, you need some way of making sure that during the peak
time, when the load is at its maximum, you have the adequate number of machines to handle the load.
Let's say for.
In this case, and during the night time, the load is less.
When the number of users are less, you can probably just have two machines running as part of your
skill set, these two machines running as part of your infrastructure.

It's not only the underlying physical infrastructure that's managed for you, it's also the underlying
virtual infrastructure, the virtual machines.
All you have to do is to create a resource based on the Azure Web App service and then upload your web
application code, and then you have a web site running in a matter of minutes.

security group, the virtual network, so on and so forth.

OBM.

You are responsible for updating the web server.
You are responsible for installing security patches on the VM itself.
It's your job, right?
So sometimes companies have a numerous number of applications and they don't want to manage even that
virtual infrastructure.

--- Azure Web Apps - Deployment Slots ---

Hi and welcome back.
Now in this chapter, I want to give an introduction onto a feature known as deployment slots.
Before we actually go on to understanding deployment slots, let's go through very basic scenario that
leads us on to why is a feature of deployment slots so relevant when it comes on to deploying newer
versions of your application?
So obviously I'd shown you in the last chapter a simple PHP page as part of the Azure Web app.
I told you, imagine that you have your development teams who have bundled the entire application code.
They give it to you as an admin, and then you publish that code onto the Azure Web app.
Now, obviously, application code goes through a lot of changes.
You would have new features being added on to the web application, you could have bug fixes, etc.
hence you will have multiple revisions, multiple versions of the application.
We all know that Taking newer versions of applications, and directly putting them or pushing them onto
production is a risky affair at any point in time.
The application code could break, it could break the application, and users will not be able to use
it.
You get bad reviews.
So there's always a cycle that needs to be maintained when it comes on to deploying newer versions of
the application.
You first would want to test the new version to make sure that it is working as expected.
If it is working as expected, then you can push that new version onto production.
How does deployment slots help us in this regard?
So let's say that we have version one of your application running on the Azure Web app.
This is your main application.
Users are using this application.
We have now a new revision.
We want to push that new revision onto the Azure Web app, the production.
But before that, we want to test that version.
Azure Web Apps has this feature known as deployment slots.
What you can do is you can create a new slot.
You can give it a name, let's say staging.
You can publish the newer version of your application onto the slot.
The slot is like an additional web app.
You can actually deploy the newer version of your code onto this web app itself.
So now you have your main application running as part of something known now as a production slot,
and you can have newer versions of your application that need to be tested, published on this new web
app on this new slot.
Now, in order to make use of deployment slots, we have to bump up the SKU of our App Service plan.
Deployment slots are only available with the standard App Service plan or higher, so for the first
step will be to upgrade our App Service plan.
We'll upgrade it onto the standard.
Once we do that, we can add a deployment slot, then we can publish a newer version of our application.
And then we have another feature available as part of deployment slots.
Once the testing of our newer version is complete, we can perform a simple swap.
So the code running in our slot can be swapped out with our production code, and the production code
would come onto our staging slot onto our deployment slot.
Then you would have the newer version of your application running in the production slot in the Azure
Web app.
The benefit of this is it's an easy switch.
The other benefit is you can roll back easily.
So by chance, in case if the newer version is broken, it's not working in the production web app,
you can do a swap again.
So you can take the prior working version of your application from the deployment slot, move it back
into production, and move the newer version back onto the slot.
So this is the benefit of using deployment slots.
Let's look at a simple example on this in the next chapter.

--- Container-based applications ---

Hi and welcome back.
Now in this particular section we have looked at a number of compute based services.
We have looked at Azure VMs.
We have looked at virtual machine scale sets.
We have seen Azure Web Apps as part of the exam objectives.
We have to also understand the different services that can be used to host some container based applications.
So before we can actually dwell into using the various services, I first want to give a quick introduction
to students who are not aware of the, you know, the fact of having container based applications in
place.
Now, we are all well aware of the concept of virtual machines.
Virtual machines were designed to make the most of the hardware specifications of the underlying physical
machine.
You could have multiple virtual machines hosted on the same physical server, and you could make use
of the underlying hardware specifications of the physical server for your VMs, and then you have your
applications hosted on VMs itself.
So companies would deploy multiple applications on, let's say, the same virtual machine just to make
the most out of the hardware.
But the problem was that, you know, there were some inherent problems when it came onto hosting applications
on virtual machines.
Let's say you had two applications hosted on the same VM.
So you have a physical server.
You have your host OS.
You have a hypervisor based software that will allow you to virtualize the physical infrastructure.
And then you host your virtual machines.
So let's say you have two applications hosted on the same VM.
Let's say that one of the applications requires an update at the OS level at the virtual machine OS
level.
There's some library that you install or update.
This is required by the first application.
Now because of the installation of that library, it could cause a problem with the other application
running on the same VM.
So here the problem is that when you're making an update to the VM for one application, it might interfere
with other applications running on the same VM.
So this is one inherent problem.
The other problem was that, you know, you could have applications running on a VM in your dev environment.
When you move it onto a VM in the prod environment it would not work.
This could be because of the differences in configuration at an OS level, maybe at an application level
between the dev and prod environment.
So these were the some inherent problems which were still there when it came on to hosting applications
on virtual machines.
Then we came to the advent of container based applications.
So this is a very popular tool set known as Docker.
Docker allows you to package your application into something known as Docker based images.
And then you can run those Docker based images has containers here.
The architecture is quite simple.
You again have your virtual machines.
But then on the VM on the virtual machine.
Here I'm showing an example of a physical server, but on a physical server or a VM.
You can install something known as the container engine.
You then package your application into something known as a container and run it on the container engine.
Here each container has only the application code and whatever dependencies are required for the application
to run within the container itself.
So if you had the application required any update, you would make that update only to that container
running the application so each container could run independently on the virtual machine itself.
This was just a quick intro.
Now, we do have a lot of chapters ahead because we understand in depth how do we make use of services
on Azure for deploying container based applications?

--- Lab - Setting up Docker on an Azure virtual machine ---

Now in order to see how we can make use of services on Azure.
When it comes on to hosting container based applications, I'm going to take an approach wherein I'm
first going to see how to use Docker on an Azure VM.
Again, this is for those students who are not familiar with creating something known as Docker image,
creating something known as Docker container.
I want you all to understand in depth how to make use of the container based services on Azure.

--- Lab - Azure Container Registry Service ---

Now in the prior chapter, what we've done is we have built something known as a Docker image.

Not the most safest approach when it comes onto sharing Docker based images.
See, what we've done as a developer is we've built our own Docker image.
Let's say it's a full blown application.
You now need to run that application on another target environment.
For this you need the Docker image.
Currently the only way to run the container on the target machine is to copy the Docker image from our
source onto the target.
Well, what you can do is instead of doing this, you can publish your image, your Docker image, or
to a public container image registry that's known as Docker Hub.
Docker hub actually hosts millions of Docker images.
That includes a host of official images for Linux, databases, programming languages, etc. so one
option is developers can push their application images onto Docker Hub, and then from the target machine,
they can pull down the image from Docker Hub and run a container.
But in Azure there is another option known as the Azure Container Registry Service.
So what we can do is we can build A resource based on the service, and we can push our Docker image
onto the container registry.
The Azure Container Registry Service is a managed private Docker registry.
We can push our container images there.
The key features are.
It's a private storage for your images within Azure itself.
You have the ability to integrate with Microsoft Android for security.
And you have other aspects like network security as well.

--- Azure Container Apps ---

Hi and welcome back.
Now in this chapter, I want to give kind of a brief overview of something known as Azure Container
Apps.
We have seen how we could run our containers.
We saw how we could run a PHP application.
We saw how we could run a MySQL database container within a service known as the Azure Container Instance
Service.
This is actually the most simplest way to run your container there.
You don't need to provision any infrastructure.
Remember, you just specify the amount of virtual CPUs and the amount of memory that will be provisioned
for you.
But normally in an application for a company, they would have multiple containers for the application.
We just you know, ours is very simple.
We have two containers, an app container and a database container.
But typically for an application you will have different containers.
Here I'm giving an example of just four containers.
You could have the web front end container that is responsible for serving the front end web UI to your
users.
You might have again the database container.
You might have a separate API container that exposes APIs that calls other functions.
You might have one container that's only used for caching purposes.
You could have multiple containers for your application.
In such cases, it would not be wise to go ahead and use the Azure Container Instance service for hosting
these containers.
You would need to look at a container orchestration software.
You might have heard of a tool known as Kubernetes.
This is a very popular tool when it comes on to running your container based applications.
Here what you do is you actually provision a cluster of machines.
You install Kubernetes, and then you submit your deployments for your container based applications.
You have basically one machine that is the Kubernetes controller that serves the control plane.
Your containers run on nodes within the cluster.
Kubernetes has a software has several features that includes schedule and placement.
So Kubernetes will take care of choosing which node to run your container.
Self-healing.
So if a container crashes, it would reschedule the container on a healthy node.
Scaling it could create replicas based on demand.
It had support for routing of traffic.
And also you could implement different patterns in terms of deployment.
So there's a lot of features available in Kubernetes.
So normally if you had kind of a really multi container application and you wanted the entire orchestration
process in place, you could make use of Kubernetes.
Azure Container Apps is just an abstraction layer built on top of Kubernetes.
So in the end you are making use of Kubernetes as a software.
But there you don't need to provision the underlying infrastructure.
It's managed for you.
You don't need to install the software that is managed for you.
It just a layer on top of it.
That is in a nutshell, what is Azure Container Apps?
We are going to look at a very simple deployment on Azure Container Apps using our images that we have
in Azure Container Registry.
But just before that, if you want to look at some key terms in Azure Container app.
So first we have the Azure Container App environment.
This is a secure boundary that contains one or more container apps.
So apps in the same environment can talk internally to each other.
Then you have the container app itself.
So you can deploy multiple container apps to the same container app environment.
Then you have revisions.
You can have different versions of your applications running across different revisions of each container
app.
And then you have replicas.
This is the running instance of a revision in the next chapter.
Let's look at a quick demo on using Azure Container Apps.

--- Networking 101 - Networks, devices and IP addresses - Basics ---

Hi and welcome on to this section.
So in this section we are going to be covering the networking aspect when it comes onto the AZ 104 exam.
But first, just for the benefit of those students who are not familiar from a networking aspect, I
want to go through a few chapters to cover some basic aspects.
So for example, I want to cover what exactly is a network, what are IP addresses, so on and so forth.
And then we'll start moving on to building virtual networks on Azure.
So what is a network.
A network is just devices actually talking to each other.
Plus you have addresses that help to identify the devices on the networks.
And you have rules that define how messages are sent across devices.
If you look at large organizations, what they do is they build data centers within these data centers,
they set up servers.
These servers are used for hosting applications.
You have users who use workstations.
So all of these servers, workstations, devices, etc. they have to be connected together.
They are connected via the use of a network.
You have physical switches and routers in place that help to build the network.
Switches are devices that are used to normally route traffic within a local area network.
And routers are devices that are normally used to route traffic between networks.
Even if you look at your home setup and you have your Wi-Fi router, you have your laptops and you have
your devices.
In such a case, even your home Wi-Fi router behaves as a network device.
Your laptop.
your mobile devices are all actually part of a home network.
The devices within the home network get their own private IP addresses that help to identify each device
on the network.
The home Wi-Fi router behaves as something known as the default gateway.
It gets its own IP address at the same time.
Your home Wi-Fi router also behaves as a setup that takes the traffic from, you know, the request
from your laptop, your mobile devices, etc. and routes it onto the internet.
So even at home, if you don't know it, your devices when you connect onto the home Wi-Fi router,
they're all part of a network.
In this chapter we're going to start very simple.
We want to set the premise when it comes onto what exactly is a network.

--- Networking 101 - IP addresses ---

In the prior chapter, we set kind of a base wherein we had an introduction, a simple introduction
onto networks.
In this chapter, I want to go through IP addresses.
I mentioned that for even your home network, your devices actually get assigned an IP address.
For example, you might have a laptop that might get an IP address of 192.168.0.2.
Your Wi-Fi router, which acts as a default gateway.
It gets one IP address of, let's say, 192.168.0.1.
All your devices take this as the default gateway onto the internet.
This IP address of 192.168.0.1 is visible to your devices internally, at the same time, the internet
services This provider provides you with an with a public IP address that is also a sign onto the router.
So what is this IP address.
So any time devices need to talk to each other they need to have these unique identifiers.
And that is what is an IP address.
It's a number that helps to identify a device on a network.
And it tells routers on how to send packets.
If you look at an IP address, the IP address is just basically a string of binary numbers.
It's you know, currently most devices are based on IP version four IPv4 addresses are 32 bits.
What is a bit a bit is either a representation of 0 or 1.
The IP address is split into four octets of eight bits each.
We write them in the dotted notation, wherein for example I said 192.
This would be the binary equivalent of that octet.
168.
This is the binary equivalent.
So on and so forth.
So in the end the IP address which is currently based on IP version four, we also have IP version six.
It's 32 bits in nature.
They are separated by the dot notation.
And we have four octets of eight bits each.
If we look at an IP address there are actually two parts that it is packed into one number.
One part is the network.
This identifies which network the address belongs to.
And then finally you have the address of the host.
If you take an example of a virtual machine hosted in a network, so the network has its defined address
and the virtual machine has its defined address, so that together forms the address of the virtual
machine itself.
So as an example here, 192.168.0 we can say that 192.168.0 is the network address and 20 is the address
of the host.
How do you actually come to this number?
Well, this is done via the use of.
something known as specifying either an address prefix or using a Cidr block.
So, for example, if I say that the IP address range would be or the Cidr block would be 192.168.0.0,
that means the first 24 bits.
So the first 24 bits are assigned for the network.
It's the network address, and the last eight bits are what are available for the host machines within
the network.
So in this chapter I want to go a step further.
I first want to explain what is an IP address.
What constitutes an IP address.
And then briefly we went on to the network portion of an IP address and the host portion.
Let's now move on to the next chapter.

--- Networking 101 - Subnet Mask and CIDR blocks ---

Now, in the prior chapters, we had kind of a very brief overview on the concept of having networks
in place.
We understand that devices on a network need to have an IP address, but how do we carve out one big
address space into smaller, routable chunks?
That's where we make use of something known as Cidr blocks and subnet mask.
What exactly is a Cidr block or a subnet mask?
So the subnet mask is just a 32 bit number that tells us that which part of an IP version four address,
you know, it breaks it down onto a network portion and a host portion within a mask bit is set as one.
That position belongs to the network, and if it's zero, it belongs to the host.
Has an example here.
So as an example, if I have.
An IP address range of 10.0.0.0, and we say that the subnet mask is
255.255.255.0255
means all of the eight bits are marked as one.
This also means that this entire portion the entire first set of octets three octets.
This belongs to the network, and the last octet belongs to the host.
The subnet mask is, I said, just a 30 bit number that tells us which part of the entire IP version
four address breaks it down into the network and the host portion.
Then what is the Cidr block?
So Cidr stands for classless Inter-domain routing.
It gives us another way of representing an IP address range in terms of signifying what parts are part
of the network and what parts are part of the host.
Again, if you take the similar example of 10.0.0.0 this time, if I say slash 24, this is a Cidr block.
Slash 24 means that the first 24 bits are marked again for the network, and the last eight bits are
marked for the host.
I'm giving another example here when it comes onto a Cidr block.
If we have slash 25, the subnet mask would be 55.255.255.128.
If you look at having slash 28 has the sign of prefix, the total number of IP addresses that you can
get that can be assigned is 128.
But normally as part of a network, two addresses are reserved.
One is for the network address and the other is known as the broadcast address.
In this chapter, I kind of want to give that brief overview when it comes on to having a subnet mask
in place and a Cidr block.
Obviously, when we start working with virtual networks on Azure, we're going to start building networks
and subnets and carving out IP address spaces in these first set of chapters, just for the benefit
of students who are not familiar with the concept of a network, with the concept of an IP address,
with the concept of Cidr blocks.
I want to go kind of through this basic chapters.

In this chapter let's briefly go over the concept of subnets.
The virtual networks help to define a private IP address in Azure.
The subnets help to slice the network into smaller chunks that can be managed separately.
The subnets itself have their own Cidr prefix or a Cidr block.
This is a subset of the address space of the virtual network.
With the help of subnets, we can segregate workloads.
Apply different security rules for each subnet.
You know, as an example, we could have a simple virtual network that has three subnets.
You can have one subnet that is used for hosting the web servers, another subnet for hosting the application
servers, and another subnet for hosting the database servers.
What you're doing is you are carving out different parts of the virtual network and then hosting workloads
within the subnet itself.
So you're trying to create layers within the network and then host different types of servers in each
subnet.
If we look at the address range that I've given for the subnet.
So I said let's uh, we have the address range of the virtual network here.

into smaller networks.
We are using this octet to define now our subnets.
So as you know, for if you take now the network which is a constant and the changing third octet,
what are the possible numbers that you can get.
So 1.0.0 we can get 10.0.110.0.2 all the way down, right till 254.
So now all of these can become the network address for your subnets.
I'm saying that let's now use the first 24 bits out of this range for defining our subnets.
So in this way we can start having multiple subnets all the way down.
And then within these subnets we can host our machines.
Just trying to break down the concept even further when it comes onto the usage of subnets.
I'm just giving some information based on the architecture that I have here in the web subnet, you
could host something known as application gateway machines that is getting traffic from the internet
from your users.
So this would accept traffic from the internet.
Then you have let's say the app based subnet.
This holds the virtual machines that actually host the actual application.
And you could have a database subnet that hosts your database machines.
If you're looking from a security aspect in terms of traffic routing, I say the entire purpose of having
subnets is to segregate your workloads, and then you can have rules that actually define the traffic
that's moving across these subnets.
So for the web subnet that is the front facing subnet you can have traffic coming in or allowed from
the internet.
No traffic from the internet should be allowed onto machines in the app and the database subnet.

First, what is the action?

What is a protocol?
TCP, UDP, ICMP or any?
What is the source of the request?

security group.

--- Network Watcher ---

Hi and welcome back.
Now, in the next set of chapters, I want to go through the different tools that are available in the
Azure Network Watcher service.
So the Azure Network Watcher service is an entire suite of tools that allows you to monitor and diagnose
issues when it comes onto your network.
These are monitoring tools that help you to view and monitor your resources.
You have diagnostic tools that help you to troubleshoot and diagnose networking issues.
You have tools that allow you to log and visualize your network traffic.
Some of the tools available are.
We have connection monitor.
Here you can create end to end reachability tests.
You can get alerts when connectivity or performance drifts you have connection troubleshoot.
This is a one off probe that you can define from a source to a destination, based on a port or a protocol.
We have the IP flow verify.
This allows you to check if a packet is allowed or denied to or from an Azure VM.
This is based on the rules that you set within the Network security group.
Then we have the next hop.
This gives you the next hop type the IP address, the route table ID of a specific destination IP address.
We have the effective security rules here.
You can get an overall an aggregated view of the inbound and outbound rules that apply to a network
interface.
We have packet capture.
This allows you to create packet capture sessions to track traffic to and from an Azure VM or a scale
set.
We have NSG or VNet flow logs.
This allows you to log information about traffic flowing through the virtual network or the Network
Security group.
And we have traffic analytics here.
This is a cloud based solution that provides visibility into user and application activity in your cloud
networks.
In the next set of chapters, let's see how we can work with the tools defined in Azure Network Watcher.

--- User Defined Routes ---

Hi and welcome back.
Now I want to go through the concept of having a user defined route in place.
Normally from a networking aspect, you have routes in place that enables the routing of data from a
source onto the destination.
Because he obviously devices like switches and routers, they need to understand, okay, how do we
route data from the source onto the destination?
What are the rules for your virtual network?
There are some default routes in place.
You know, that's why within a virtual network itself, if you try to send a packet of data.
So in our previous demos, when we were looking at reaching our database server from the web server,
it was quite simple.
If we use a curl command from the database server to reach the web server, it would work as expected,
as long as you have the required rule in place.
In the network security group, the energy is only used to filter the traffic, but there still should
be some rule in place to tell, you know, the underlying in the background.
There will be some virtual network device that is going to take the request from the database server
onto the web server, or from the web server onto the database server that behind the scenes network
routers, which needs to understand how to route the data.
So there are some system routes in place.
Quite simple.
If you have a source and if you have a destination, how do you route the data?
So within the virtual network, routing is already enabled, wherein any machine can route traffic to
any other machine in the network itself so that basic communication is always there.
But there are cases wherein a company might want to have a centralized VM in place, which would take
in all of the request and then forward it onto the destination accordingly.
You know, we had seen this sort of example even earlier early on in one of our earlier chapters when
we were looking at adding secondary network interfaces.
So let's say that on this machine, the company has installed some sort of firewall or network appliance
that needs to inspect all data within the virtual network.
So if you have a source machine and the source machine needs to send data onto a target, it's quite
simple.
It's kind of a direct connection because of the route.
But you might want to define a, you know, your own user defined route, which says that before the
traffic from this source can reach the target, the request needs to flow via this central subnet.
It would be processed by some machine in the subnet and then it will be directed onto the target.
I said here you could be having some packet inspection software that would inspect the request, inspect
the packet of data from a security perspective, and then it can forward the data accordingly.
So for this, you want to define a user defined route wherein you are telling how the routing of packets
should work.

--- The Azure Load Balancer Service ---

Hi and welcome back.
Now in the next set of chapters, we are going to be looking at the Azure Load Balancer service.
A load balancer is used to distribute incoming traffic across a set of back end servers.
Now, we've already understood the concept that if you have a critical application, if a company has
a revenue generating application, normally what they would do is they would host the application on
a number of VMs within a network.
They could distribute these VMs across an availability set or across availability zones.
The reason they do this is in case if one VM goes down that's holding the application, the request
from the users can actually be directed onto the other running VMs.
So there's no impact as such onto the infrastructure.
So this is the basic concept when you have an application running on multiple machines.
But then in order for the traffic to be distributed across these machines, you know, across the application
running on these machines, you need some sort of load balancing service in front.
One option is to provision machines in a new subnet.
Take a load balancing software from another vendor.
Install that load balancing software on these virtual machines and then configure them accordingly.
Then requests from the internet from the users will go via the load balancer onto the machines.
But if you don't want the burden of managing the underlying infrastructure for the load balancer itself,
what you can do is you can make use of the Azure Load Balancing service.
So in a nutshell, simply it is a managed solution where the load balancer is maintained for you.
You can use the load balancer to distribute traffic to your backend virtual machines.
And this leaves you just time to focus on your infrastructure.
This was a very quick introduction onto the purpose of a load balancer.
In the subsequent sections we are going to look at the implementation of the load balancer itself.

--- DNS Fundamentals for Azure Administrators ---

Hi and welcome back.
Now in the next set of chapters we are going to go through, how do we implement DNS via the use of
Azure based services.
But before that, just for the benefit of students who might not be familiar with DNS and bi DNS, I
mean the Domain name system, I'm going to go through some fundamentals when it comes onto DNS itself.
Now on your laptop, when you're browsing for a site, let's say at home, your request is going via
the Wi-Fi router.
Going onto the internet, let's say within the browser, you are trying to go on to the Microsoft site.
So https ww dot Microsoft.com.
Your laptop first needs to establish a connection with the underlying Microsoft servers, fetch the
content for the home page, and then the content is sent onto your laptop and then your browser renders
the content.
So a connection needs to be made between your laptop and the Microsoft servers.
Now with your laptop.
Make a connection using the name.
No, the connection is made via the use of IP addresses.
I told you, IP addresses are used to identify devices on a network.
Hence, your laptop needs to understand what is the target IP address for the Microsoft servers.
Then a connection is established and then the content of the Microsoft.com home page is sent back onto
the laptop.
How does your laptop get to know what is the IP address of the Microsoft servers?
You know, ideally in the browser, if you had to type the IP address of the servers itself, then you
could establish a connection.
But then we as humans we are more familiar with remembering names rather than IP addresses.
And hence we have this concept of a domain name system, wherein we have user friendly names or domain
names that are mapped onto IP addresses.
So how does I said all laptop when it connects or when it tries to fetch a page from a website on the
internet?
How would it get that IP address?
Well, this is why the DNS system.
It's like a phone book that helps you turn your domain names into IP addresses.
A very simple concept.
It is a mapping of at a simple term, the domain name onto your IP address.
The DNS system just hosts a set of records.
The record has that mapping.
Your laptop needs to fetch the IP address that is mapped onto the domain name from the Domain Name System.
Now, just to give a simple understanding of the steps involved when you're browsing a site, I said
first you type in the URL onto your browser.
Your browser will then formulate a query to actually resolve the domain name of, let's say, microsoft.com
from the internet.
The query would first go to your internet services provider to see if it can be resolved there.
So there are various, um, companies around the world that hold something known as name servers.
If the internet services provider cannot resolve the name, it will then forward the request onto other
domain servers across the internet.
Finally, the request would reach something known as an authoritative name server.
A name server is just a DNS server that answers DNS queries for a domain.
The IP address for the domain is then sent back onto your browser, onto your laptop, and then your
laptop makes a simple connection across the internet to the Microsoft servers via IP addresses, and
then the data is sent from the page, you know, from the external domain site onto your laptop.
This is a very, just a very, very simple explanation of the purpose of a domain name system.
In the end, it's a simple system that has a mapping of domain names into IP addresses.
Let's go on to the further chapters where in we're going to look at the workings of using DNS services
on Azure.

--- Azure Web App - Virtual Network Integration ---

Hi and welcome back.
Now, in the next set of chapters, I want to go through a feature known as the Virtual Network Integration
feature when it comes onto the Azure App Service.
In the section of compute, you know, we know that there are several ways of hosting an application.
So let's say you have a web layer and a database layer.
The web application needs to connect onto the database server.
Normally what you'll do is you'll allocate a public IP address onto the VM.
Hosting the web application.
And the database server would not have a public IP address.
Instead, the communication would be internal from the web application onto the database.
We also know that when it comes onto the web application, we could make use of a service known as the
Azure App Service or Azure Web Apps.
Now, if you do have your web application hosted using Azure Web Apps, we need to be able to connect,
let's say, to a database internally within a virtual network.
See, by default, the app service is a public service.
Hence, if the web application hosted on the Azure Web app needs to connect onto a database, that database
should be exposed also onto the internet.
But normally we have databases that are hosted within a virtual network.
If you want to have kind of private communication between the Azure Web app and the virtual network
hosting a database server, we can make use of a feature known as the Virtual Network Integration feature.
This allows access from the web app resources in the virtual to resources in the virtual network.
But please note that the other way is not possible.
So yes, the Azure Web app can talk to resources in the virtual network, but no resources within the
virtual network can initiate an outbound communication with the Azure Web app.
Now, when it comes to the App Service plan, this feature requires the basic App Service plan or higher.
This feature also requires the virtual network to be in the same region as the App Service, to enable
virtual network integration.
An empty dedicated subnet in the virtual network.
This subnet is used by the Virtual Network Integration feature.
So let's move on to the subsequent chapters.
I want to showcase a demo on how we can make use of this feature.

--- Introduction to Azure Storage Accounts ---

Hi and welcome on to the section.
Now in this section we are going to cover a very important Azure service and that is known as Azure
Storage Accounts.
In the section of compute yes, we covered a lot of important services like Azure VMs, virtual machines,
scale sets, etc. in this complete section we are focusing on Azure Storage accounts.
This is actually the fundamental building block for storage on Azure.
It actually provides a secure, highly available and scalable way to store different kinds of data.
So within a storage account you can have actually access to multiple services.
There is a service known as the blob service.
This is used for storing unstructured data like images, documents, videos, etc. you have file shares.
This is a fully managed file share on the cloud that you can access using the standard file protocols,
we have the Cue service, a very simple messaging service for communication between application components.
And then we have the table service.
The table service is used for storing structured non-relational data.

--- Azure Storage - Blob service - Different authorization techniques ---

Now, in this chapter, I want to give an overview on the different authorization techniques that are
available for accessing your data within Azure Storage.
You've already seen one technique that is giving anonymous access.
What we have to remember at the core is the Azure Blob service.
The storage account is a public service.
So from my laptop via the internet, I'm able to access the objects within the blob service.
We had seen how to enable ourselves to access the blobs via the use of anonymous access.
Not the most secure approach in case.
If you do have a container that hosts images or a static website that should be available for all users
at that point in time, you can yes, enable anonymous access.
But normally this is disabled by default.
Another way to authorize users to access data is via the use of key authorization.
Each storage account gets two access keys.
These are like your passwords.
They are long strings.
They will give you access to all data within the storage account.
So again this is not the most preferred approach when it comes on to giving access, because this is
like a master password for your storage account, wherein you get access to all services and all data
within the storage account.
Then we come to the more secure ways of authorization.
One is via the use of shared access signatures.
You can generate temporary fine grained tokens.
These tokens can limit the access for the resources based on what service to access based on permissions,
and there are various aspects in which you can limit the aspects in which we can limit the access to
resources.
This is ideal for giving short term access to your data.
And then we have access based on Microsoft Entra ID.
In this particular section we will not focus on Microsoft and ID.
We will do this in the section of security because I want to first go through Microsoft and ID, and
then we'll go through giving access to storage accounts.
So we'll just cover using access keys for now and using shared access signatures.
This is to give an overview.
Let's move on to the next chapters and see how we can make use of these different authorization mechanisms.

And there's one last note in terms of the condition of the days after the last tear change greater than.
C let's say that you have an object, and based on a particular rule, it was moved to the archive access
tier.
But there was a reason that you had to rehydrate that particular object.
Now when you rehydrate that object, it does not update the last modified or the last access time.
So what could happen is after you rehydrate the object, the rule which is already existing might kick
in again and re archive the object and it will go in a loop.
So what you can do is you can add that additional kind of condition, saying that the age in days after
there was a tier, a tier change in the particular blob.
So a lot of things to consider when you're creating lifecycle management rules in these sort of chapters.
I want to go through these important points on how you define these rules.

--- What are Azure Resource Manager templates ---

So in this section we are now going to focus on building something known as ARM templates.
That's Azure Resource Manager templates.
In the prior sections we have looked at numerous examples on building resources within Azure.
We have seen how to build virtual machines, how to build storage accounts, so on and so forth.
Normally in companies you would need to build a full application environment in Azure, where in you
could have a set of machines, you could have a set of storage accounts, you could have other services
like Azure SQL databases, so on and so forth.
At the same time, you might need to rebuild these environments for let's say dev or test for UAT for
prod, trying to build numerous resources via the use of the Azure portal itself.
Using the wizard can be, you know, can become tedious over time if you want to make your actions repeatable
in nature.
You want to audit them.
You want to have consistent deployments.
We can make use of ARM based templates.
Azure Resource Manager templates.
An ARM template is a declarative, JSON based file that describes the desired state of your Azure resources.
Hence, within your ARM template you would declare okay, what should be the state of the virtual network?
So you want to have a virtual network in Azure with a particular name, with a particular IP address
prefix, where a set of subnets, so on and so forth.
You want to have a VM based on let's say ubuntu.
You would define that in your ARM based template.
Then once you have these template deployments in place, all you need to do is you need to submit these
templates aren't, Azure Resource Manager, and Azure Resource Manager would deploy the resources based
on the definition of a template.
Some of the benefits of maintaining templates are.
So firstly consistency.
You can define the same blueprint when it comes onto your dev your test or your prod environments.
Speed.
Instead of going through the wizard over and over again for building different resources, you can build
them much more faster via the use of a code base file.
Another is auditing.
You can maintain different versions of your code file, and it also helps you define kind of an audit
trail when it comes onto your resources deployed.
We are going to go through examples on deploying resources in Azure based on ARM based templates.
In this chapter one have that quick introduction.

--- ARM Template structure ---

In this chapter, I briefly want to go through the structure of an ARM template.
So obviously these templates are going to have some sort of structure, because when you submit these
templates onto Azure, based on the structure of the template, Azure will go ahead and define your
resources accordingly.
In the Microsoft documentation, you can see the basic template format.
In the template format we have the schema.
The schema is just a URL that tells, let's say tools like Visual Studio Code how to validate the JSON
based documents.
Then we have the content version.
This is a free form version string that you can define.
It does not affect the behavior of the deployment of the resources in Azure.
It is just a way for a team to collaborate on changes that are happening within the template itself,
by maintaining different versions.
Our main.
The main heart of your template is the resources section.
In the resources section, you declare the different resources that you want to create or update within
Azure.
In resources, you will define the type of resource that you want to, you know, create in Azure,
what is the name, location, so on and so forth.
We can define variables.
These are kind of local values in your template.
You can define them once and then reuse it within the template.
You can define it once and reuse it within the template itself.
We have parameters.
These are values that you can pass at the deployment time of the template.
So let's say you want to specify the region for the deployment of resources.
Instead of hard coding the region in the template you can pass.
The region has a value during the deployment time itself.
This is the basic template structure.
Obviously, in the subsequent chapters, when we start going through building ARM based templates,
you'll get a better understanding.
If you want to get an overview, go through this documentation link to understand about the basic ARM
template structure.

Now the problem is the dependency across resources.
See our VM needs a primary network interface.

For the VM to exist for the network interface what is required.
The virtual network.
So the virtual network should also be in place beforehand.
What do you think is the execution?

How does Resource Manager actually execute the ARM template?

So here the first resource is the storage account.
The next is the virtual network.
Then after that we have the public IP address.
Do you think that Azure Resource Manager based on this ARM template it will go order by order sequentially
in this file.
The answer is no.
It will take in this ARM template and in any order it will start deploying resources.
Now the problem is that it could be currently like deploying the network interface, the virtual network
and probably the VM.
Let's say that the VM is in the process of being deployed.
But the problem is that the network is still not in place.
The network interface is not in place.
Your ARM template will run into an error because I told you that in order for the VM to exist, for
the VM to be deployed, the virtual network should exist first and even the network interface.
So there is a dependency across resources.
By default, ARM will try its best to understand this dependency, but it will not always be the case
that everything will work as expected.
You cannot expect ARM to automatically or magically understand what is the dependency across all resources.
So now with this clean slate, if I run my template, this dependency dot JSON, If I go on to the terminal

It might not work.

network interface and then the VM.
But there are cases where it could run into an error.
And that's because it would probably tell you that there's a problem in creating the VM, because the
virtual network does not exist, or the network interface does not exist.
Hence, we need to explicitly tell ARM that there is a dependency across resources.

--- Azure Storage Service Encryption ---

In this chapter, I briefly just want to go through Azure Storage Encryption.
Since Azure Storage is a critical service in which companies store their data, which could be critical
in nature, encryption at rest is very important.
Now, by default, Azure Storage does use server side encryption to automatically encrypt your data
when it is persisted onto the cloud.
So, for example, if I go on to an existing Azure storage account, there is a section on encryption.
Within encryption we can see that it is already enabled.
We are making use of Azure Storage by default.
Makes use of Microsoft managed keys in its default state.
We can enable support for customer managed keys for blobs and files only.
In this current state, we can select customer managed keys and we can make use of an encryption key
defined in an Azure Key Vault.
So something that we can do now apart from Azure Storage encryption at rest we also have something known
as encryption scopes.
Scopes allow you to manage encryption again with your own encryption key defined in Azure Key Vault.
But this time that key can be scoped onto a container or an individual blob.
So in.
If you do want to use the key for the entire Azure Storage account, because sometimes you might have,
let's say multiple departments in your company, and each department has their own container of data
within Azure Storage, and each department might manage their own encryption key within the key vault.
Hence you can make use of encryption scopes to only.
Hence, you can make use of encryption scopes that only scope a particular encryption key to a particular
container, or even onto a particular blob.
Let's look at an example on just making use of encryption scopes.
Now when it comes on to your keyword.
So you have to make sure that soft delete is enabled.
We have to also enable purge protection.
So if I go on to purge protection I will enable this and click on save.
Something that is required.
We have our existing keyword in place right.
I'll go on to keys and we create a new encryption key.
I'll just give a simple key name and click on create.
Next when it comes onto your Azure Storage account, if I go on to encryption scopes let me click on
add.
I'll give a simple scope name.
I want to make use of customer managed keys.
Let me select my key vault and select my encryption key.

--- What is Microsoft Entra ID ---

What is Microsoft Azure ID?
So Microsoft Enter ID is it was formerly known as Azure Active Directory.

It provides the facility of authentication authenticating a user.

the act of authorization.

Do you have access to resources within an Azure subscription?

forth to manage resources.

The security based groups assign permissions.

Applications.
So as an example, within Microsoft Android you can define cloud only based users.

--- Resource tags ---

In this chapter, I want to go through the feature that's known as resource tagging.
Resource tags are nothing but key value pairs that you can assign to your resources, your resource
groups, and your subscriptions.
These tags can actually add more business context to your resources.
For example, I could add a tag of environment is equal to dev, environment is equal to prod.
Department is equal to logistics.
The benefit of tags are so we can filter resources based on the tags.
We can also group and filter spends based on the tags tags that are assigned at the resource group level.
They are not inherited.
They are not I confirm not inherited by the resources within the resource group.
So here as as an example, let's say for a company that has an Azure subscription, they have two resource
groups.
One, you know they are based on environment.
So here they have segregated their resources via resource groups based on embodiments, they have one
for dev and they have one for prod.
If they want to further segregate, they want to further add business value to their resources.
So they could say that this machine okay, is actually part of a cost center in an organization you
can have in an organization, you can have multiple cost centers.
So this machine, whatever billing is applied for, this machine needs to go against this cost center.
Similarly, you could have another machine that goes against another cost center.
Now adding tags is very simple.
If you go on to a resource within Azure, there's something known as tags.
And you can just add a tag.
Now what I've done is I've already added a tag of cost center 1702.
Here we could add another tag of let's say what type of tier is being hosted by this application.
Let's say it's a tier two and click on apply.
So just a simple name value pair.
One of the benefits of this is if I go out all resources, we should be able to apply a filter based
on tags.
So here, since I applied the cost center tag earlier on, I can choose Cost center and say that only
show me the resources that apply onto this particular cost center.
Also from a costing perspective, from a cost management perspective.
When I go onto cost analysis.
So under cost analysis, if I go to the accumulated costs and I'm getting the actual cost, but in the
group by if I scroll down, we can also filter based on the tags.
Now this year I am not getting my cost center tag.
It does take time.
I just assign the tag probably an hour ago.
You need some expense to go against the resource to go against the tag to come up here.
But you know, the benefit of resource tags are that you could filter your resources based on tags and
also from a costing perspective.
