--- Lab - Locking Resources ---

Hi and welcome back.
In this chapter, I want to go through the concept of being able to lock your Azure base resources to
protect your infrastructure.
As an administrator, you can lock an Azure subscription, an entire resource group, or just a resource
to prevent the accidental user deletion or modification of a resource.
There are two types of locks that you can define.
One is a cannot delete lock.
That means only authorized users can read and modify a resource, but they can't delete them.
You have a read only lock.
That means that authorized users can read a resource, but they can't delete or update the resource
itself.
When you apply a lock at a parent, scope or resources within that lock inherit the same lock itself.
So as an example, if I go onto Azure, if I go on to a virtual machine, just as an example, most
resources have that concept of applying locks.
If I search for locks.
It comes on the settings.
I can add a lock.
This can be either a read only or a delete based lock.
If I choose read only and just give a simple lock name and click on okay.
This lock is at the scope of the virtual machine.
Now if I go on to the overview of the machine itself, let me try to stop the machine.
This is failing because it cannot perform a write operation on the machine itself.
This is because of that read only lock.
We can also apply a lock at the resource group level.
Now if you do apply a lock at the resource group level, you have to understand that it will be inherited
by all locks within the resource group itself.
If I give a lock name, this is of the type read only and click on okay.
So what we're doing is we are creating a look at the resource group level.
Now within the resource group, if I go, for example, onto my Azure storage account, that is actually
part of that resource group.
If I search for lock, what you notice is that it has inherited the lock that we defined at the resource
group level.
On this page, you know, you can actually go through and understand the considerations before applying
your locks.

--- Management Groups ---

Hi and welcome back.

In a company they might have not only two, they could have ten.

assigning permissions and policy assignments.
The costing and budgets can also be managed per subscription.
Now, when you do have multiple subscriptions in place, you can use something known as management groups.
Management groups actually sits on top of the subscriptions.
You get a hierarchy for defining then role based access control and Azure policies.
See, what you can do is you can define something known as a management group.
You can assign subscriptions onto the group itself.
You could then have a role assign at the management group level.
Once you do this, that role will be given to the child subscription.
So each subscription will then inherit that role based access control.
So maybe by default for every subscription you might want to have some sort of roles already defined
for certain administrators like global administrators.
You could assign that role at a management group level, and then that role would come onto each and
every subscription.
Or maybe you want to have something known as a policy.
Now we'll be covering policies in a separate chapter.
When you define a policy at the management group level, then it will trickle down onto the relevant
subscriptions.
I just want to give kind of an overview on using management groups.

--- What is a Log Analytics Workspace ---

Hi and welcome back.
Now in this chapter, I want to give a brief introduction on something known as a Log analytics workspace.
Then in the subsequent chapters we'll see how to work with this particular resource type.
The log workspace is nothing but a centralized data store where you can collect your resource and your
platform logs.
What we are going to see as an example is we are going to stream logs from our Azure VMs onto a log
analytics workspace.
Sometimes from an admin perspective, from a security perspective, you want to have a central place
for pushing logs.
You can then analyze those logs over time.
Hence the log analytics workspace is that centralized data store that you can use for collecting your
resource and your logs.
You can then query for those logs using something known as a Kusto custom query language Kql.
To collect information from VMs, we would need to use something known as an Azure Monitoring Agent.
We can define data collection rules that can tell to take data, the log data from VMs, and send it
on to the Log Analytics workspace.
The monitoring agent that gets installed on each machine can then be used to collect that data and send
it on to the workspace.
So in the end, the service is very, very simple.
It is to provide a centralized logging solution for your resources.
And then you can query over the data using a language known as Kql or the Kusto query language.
Let's move on to the next chapter and perform the very simple activity of creating something known as
a log analytics workspace.

--- What is the Azure Backup feature ---

Hi and welcome back.
In the next set of chapters, we are going to look at how do we protect our workloads when it comes
onto virtual machines, especially we look at how we use the Azure Backup feature when it comes to taking
a backup of workloads running on our VMs.
We'll also be looking at the recovery services part as well.
Now, first and foremost, what is Azure Backup.
This is a cloud native solution that allows you to take backups of the entire VMs, or just the disk
attached to the machine.
You can then restore the data based on different recovery points.
This allows you to recover from accidental deletes if the VMs, for example, get infected with ransomware
or something happens to the machine itself.
If you have a backup in place, you can recover from that backup.
You can define when the backup needs to be taken via something known as a schedule.
The backups are stored in something known as a recovery services vault.
What we'll be doing initially is we'll be creating something known as a recovery services vault.
This is a separate resource on Azure when a backup is taken via the Azure Backup service.
The backups are finally stored in the vault itself.
If we look at the overall process of using the backup feature, we first need to enable backup for an
Azure Virtual Machine, wherein we assign a backup policy.
In this policy, you can define the schedule for the backup.
Is it on an hourly basis, a daily basis, or a weekly basis?
Add these scheduled time based on the policy.
Azure backup takes a snapshot of each match disk.
So this is your OS and your data.
This you also get access to something known as an instance restore.
Snapshots, which are maintained locally for faster restores and backups, are then finally stored in
the Recovery Services vault.
In the next chapters, let's look at how do we make use of Azure Backup feature.
First and foremost, we'll create the Recovery Services Vault.
Then we'll enable the backup for one of the Azure VMs that we have.
We'll then backup the Azure VM itself.
And then finally we look at the different restore operations that we have.
So let's move ahead.

--- Azure Site Recovery ---

Hi and welcome back.
In this chapter, I want to give an introduction when it comes on to Azure Site Recovery.
And then later on we'll see how to enable replication for Azure VM.
Azure Site Recovery is Azure's disaster recovery service.
This service can replicate workloads from a primary onto a secondary location.
You can replicate workloads on Azure VMs or from your on premises servers as well.
Onto Azure.
Azure Site recovery again makes use of a Recovery Services vault for replication.
When you compare this with the backup process, we get a lower recovery point objective and a lower
recovery time objective.
Okay, now what is the entire purpose behind Azure site recovery?
Now let's consider that you have enabled.
Let's go back onto Azure backup.
Let's say you've conducted a backup of an Azure VM.
Now we do know that the backup does take time.
Okay.
That's the first thing.
Depends upon the amount of data that you have on the VM itself on the disk.
Secondly a backup can be taken once or twice in a day.
So let's say that you take a backup at 9 a.m. in the morning.
Okay.
And the backup is completed by, let's say, ten.
So now you have data till ten in the morning, somewhat around that time, a little bit before that
of the VM.
And then you keep on, let's say adding data, changing the data on the VM itself.
Now if the VM crashes for any reason let's say at ten in the night and you need to recover data.
All the data between this time is lost.
The only backup that you have is before ten, right?
So all of this data is lost.
You will need to go ahead and selectively recover this data, some in some form or the other.
So here the recovery point objective right.
It's a little bit further down the line because you cannot recover anything that's closer to the time
that the VM crashed.
Another thing is the time.
When you want to recover from a backup.
Now for us the restores work quite fast because we don't have much running on our VMs.
But when you have large workloads running on VMs, the restore operation can again take time.
It could take ten minutes, 20 minutes, half an hour if a company is running a critical workload on
a set of machines, and they need to recover as soon as possible with backup and restore.
The problem is they cannot recover to the most recent point in time.
That's one problem.
Secondly, it takes time with Azure site recovery.
What you can do is let's consider a VM in East US.
You can continuously replicate data onto a secondary region.
What's the benefit.
So the first is the recovery point objective.
So here the data is continuously being transferred from the source onto the destination.
So it's not only about backups being taken at one time.
It's like at every time.
Whatever is the change data is being replicated on to the destination.
Let's say that this VM goes down.
You can quickly recover a new VM because you have the most recent data.
And since the data is already present within no time, you can get your secondary machine up and running.
So from a recovery point objective and a recovery time objective, it's low because you can recover

Based Resources and your applications.
Here it can ingest the platform, the application signals, you can store them as metrics.
And within a log analytics workspace you can analyze the log analytics tables of data with Kql, the
custom query language.
You can act using alerts, action groups, and automation.
We have the activity log that records the control plane events in your subscriptions.
Every create update delete operation on Azure Resources is recorded here.
You can use it to investigate deletions, policy effects, and service health incidents for retention
and analytics.
You can export it via the diagnostic settings to a Log Analytics workspace and Azure Storage Account,
or an event hub.
When it comes onto the Azure Monitoring Alerts.
Alerts, turns, metrics and logs and platform events into notifications.
We can define an alert based on different signal types.
For example, we have alerts based on metrics.
This can be based on the metrics emitted from your Azure based resources.
We have metrics that can be defined on activity log or even alerts based on the data coming in in a
log at workspace.
We can define the scope, the condition, the frequency and severity, and then have an action group
in place for email, SMS, logic apps, etc. We can also use action rules to mute alert notifications
during maintenance or expected noise without turning the alerts off.
The Log Analytics workspace is an Azure Monitor data store for logs.
Here, your Azure resources your servers can send its telemetry and log data onto this workspace.
You can then query the data via the use of Kql or the custom query language.
You can visualize the data using workbooks and trigger log alerts.
Here you pay based per the ingested gigs.
You can set daily caps and retention to make sure that your machines actually send data onto the Log
Analytics workspace.
Use the Azure Monitoring Agent on Windows and Linux.
We then define data collection rules.
This defines what to collect.

can send it on to the Log Analytics workspace.

This goes on to an events table.

We can collect performance counters.
We can collect logs or even logs in just via custom applications.

premise and other cloud workloads.
You have the Recovery Services Vault that is used for storing the backup data.
We have the backup vault that can be used in scenarios like Azure Disk Backup and Azure Blob Backup
recovery services.
Vault stores the VM recovery point and has policies.
Azure backup snapshots the VM and moves the data backup data onto the Recovery Services Vault.
Azure backup enables the backup extension on the VM, takes a snapshot, and then transfers the data
onto the recovery services.
Vault has a recovery point.
